source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 9 (Harmful factors and management), section 9.1.4.1 (Tungro disease). No elibrary URL visible.
text: This entry addresses the verification requested in Batch 9's flagged entry (disease_leafhopper_virus_group_FLAGGED.json) by cross-checking against Batch 10's confirmed tungro symptom set. This CARDI source confirms that Cambodia's tungro disease (ជម្ងឺទង់ក្រ： 'Tungro diseases') is transmitted by the Green leafhopper (ព្រុងសម ('sap-sucking insect'), described in the source as 'Green leafhoppers' without a single specific scientific name given - likely referring to Nephotettix virescens and/or related green leafhopper species, the vectors documented in the wider rice-tungro literature, though this CARDI source itself does not print the Latin binomial). The leafhopper can acquire the virus after feeding on an infected plant for as little as 1-5 days and can then transmit it to healthy plants, with visible tungro symptoms (yellow-orange leaf discoloration, stunting) typically appearing within about 7-10 days of a successful transmission event. Recommended control mirrors general leafhopper/virus management: clear volunteer rice and weed hosts between seasons, adjust planting time to avoid peak leafhopper activity, and use carbofuran-based insecticide only where vector populations are heavy.
caveat: This source did not print a specific Latin binomial for the 'Green leafhopper' vector, only the common name - so while the vector identity (green leafhopper, as opposed to brown planthopper) is now confirmed and distinguishable from the grassy/ragged stunt vector (brown planthopper, see the companion CARDI_CONFIRMED entry from this same batch), the exact species-level scientific name for Cambodia's tungro-vectoring green leafhopper remains unconfirmed from this particular source and would need a dedicated entomology reference to pin down precisely (e.g. Nephotettix virescens is the vector most commonly cited in the regional/IRRI literature, but this should be verified against a source that names it explicitly for Cambodia before treating it as confirmed).
